passages.title: Seeking refuge in the Lord of daybreak from all evils
passages.tafsir:
This sūrah is a single, complete prayer of refuge: the believer is commanded to place himself under the protection of the Lord of the daybreak, first from evil in general, then from three specific evils — the enveloping night, the sorcery of those who blow on knots, and the envier. It was revealed as one remedy, together with Sūrah al-Nās, at a moment when the Prophet ﷺ himself needed exactly this protection.

## The story behind the sūrah

The Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, whose narratives here are adapted from Ibn Kathir, relates the occasion of revelation. A man named Labid ibn Aʿṣam cast a spell on the Prophet ﷺ. The hadith al-Bukhari records describes him as "a man from the tribe of Banu Zurayq who is an ally of the Jews, and a hypocrite," while Maʿārif's account of the Musnad narration speaks of him simply as a Jew who worked magic on the Prophet ﷺ — the two descriptions sit side by side in the sources. According to a narration in the Musnad of Ahmad, the resulting illness lasted six months. Al-Bukhari records the account from ʿĀʼishah: the Prophet ﷺ was affected until he would sometimes think he had done something he had not done. Then one day he told her that Allah had answered him concerning what he had asked. Two men came to him in a dream — one sat by his head, the other by his feet — and between them unfolded the diagnosis: "He is bewitched." "Who bewitched him?" "Labid bin Aʿṣam… with a comb and hair from the comb… in the dried bark of a male date palm under a rock in a well called Dharwan."

The Prophet ﷺ went to the well and said, "This is the well I was shown" — its water as if henna had been soaked in it, its palm trees like the heads of devils — and removed the object. In the narration Imam Thaʿlab relates, the sorcerer had tied eleven knots on a string; the two sūrahs of refuge were revealed, comprising eleven verses, and the Prophet ﷺ recited one verse at a time, untying one knot with each, until he felt freed.

Two details of this story teach as much as the sūrah itself. First, ʿĀʼishah asked, "Will you not make this public?" He replied that Allah had cured him and he hated to spread wickedness among the people — Maʿārif notes he did not want to be the cause of anyone's harm, and though he knew the culprit, who continued attending his gatherings, no sign of complaint ever appeared on his face. Second, some are troubled that magic could touch a prophet at all. Maʿārif answers: magic operates through physical causes, and prophets were never immune to physical causes — fire burns them, fever afflicts them. Being affected in the body says nothing against prophethood.

## "Lord of the daybreak" — why this name of Allah

The word *al-falaq* (ayah 1) comes from a root meaning "to split or cleave," and here means the break of dawn — the moment light splits the darkness open. Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Jabir, "Al-Falaq is the morning," and the same is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujahid, Saʿīd bin Jubayr, al-Hasan, Qatādah and others. Al-Qurazi, Ibn Zayd and Ibn Jarir connected it to Allah's saying "He is the Cleaver of the daybreak" (6:96).

Why appeal to *this* attribute when seeking refuge? Maʿārif (citing Mazhari) explains: the darkness of night is when evils gather, and daylight scatters them. The One who splits the night with dawn every single morning is the One who can split apart any darkness that closes over you. The choice of name is itself a promise: whoever seeks protection in Allah, He will remove all afflictions from him.

## One general refuge, then three specific evils

Ayah 2 — "from the evil of whatever He has created" — already covers everything. Ibn Kathir says it means the evil of all created things; Thabit al-Bunani and al-Hasan al-Basri mentioned "Hell, Iblis and his progeny" among them. ʿAllāmah Ibn al-Qayyim, quoted in Maʿārif, observes that *sharr* (evil) has two senses: the pains and afflictions that strike a person directly, and the causes that lead to them — unbelief and sins. Everything the Qurʼan and Sunnah teach us to seek refuge from falls under one of these two.

Maʿārif then explains the structure: ayah 2 was sufficient, but three evils are singled out in ayat 3–5 because they so often cause harm.

**The dark night (ayah 3).** *Ghāsiq* derives from *ghasaq*, intense darkness; *waqaba* means for darkness to overspread completely. The early authorities differed on the referent, and Ibn Kathir lays out the views: Mujahid said the *ghāsiq* is the night — al-Bukhari mentioned this from him — and Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Qurazi, al-Hasan, Qatādah and others said it is the night when it advances with its darkness; al-Zuhri said the sun when it sets; a report from Abu Hurayrah says the star; Ibn Zayd relates that the Arabs connected it to the declining of the Pleiades, when illness would increase. Ibn Jarir said others held it to be the moon, supported by a hadith Imam Ahmad recorded in which the Prophet ﷺ showed ʿĀʼishah the rising moon and said, "Seek refuge with Allah from the evil of this *ghāsiq* when it becomes dark" — recorded also by al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasaʼi. On the reading that it is the night, Ibn al-Qayyim (quoted in Maʿārif) explains why it is singled out: night is when the jinn, harmful creatures, thieves and attacking enemies emerge, and when black magic is at its worst — and as dawn approaches, the effects of all these things fade away.

**The blowers on knots (ayah 4).** Mujahid, ʿIkrimah, al-Hasan, Qatādah and al-Dahhak said this means the witches, who tie knots, recite incantations and blow on them — precisely what was done to the Prophet ﷺ. The word is feminine; Maʿārif notes it may stand for "evil souls" (covering men and women alike), or refer to women specifically, perhaps because Labid had the act carried out through his daughters. Why single out sorcery? Because it struck the Prophet ﷺ in this very story, and because its victims usually do not recognise it — they assume a medical ailment and seek medical cures while the harm deepens.

**The envier (ayah 5).** *Hasad* is the wish that another person be stripped of a blessing Allah gave him. Maʿārif distinguishes it sharply from *ghibṭah* — wanting the same blessing for yourself without wanting the other to lose it, which is permissible and even desirable. Hasad is a major sin, and (as Qurtubi notes) the first sin ever committed: Iblis envied Adam in heaven, and Qabil envied his brother Habil on earth. It is singled out here because envy was the engine of the whole episode — the Jews and hypocrites could not bear Islam's rapid rise, could not defeat the Prophet ﷺ openly, so they turned to witchcraft. The envier is restless day and night, always seeking his target's loss.

Maʿārif's concluding observation explains a subtle asymmetry in the wording. The night is qualified — "*when* it penetrates" — because darkness harms only when it fully overspreads. The envier is qualified — "*when* he envies" — because envy harms its object only once the envier acts on it in word or deed; until then his resentment burns only himself. But the witches carry no qualifier, because the harm of sorcery is general.

## The rank of these two sūrahs

Ibn Kathir gathers remarkable hadith on al-Falaq and al-Nās together — the *Muʿawwidhatayn*, "the two sūrahs of seeking refuge." Muslim records in his Sahih from ʿUqbah bin ʿĀmir that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Do you not see that there have been Ayat revealed to me tonight the like of which has not been seen before?" — these two sūrahs. In another narration recorded by al-Nasaʼi, he said, "Verily, the people do not seek protection with anything like these two," and to Ibn ʿĀbis al-Juhani he named them the best thing that those who seek protection use for protection.

He also taught them practically. He told ʿUqbah, in the hadith recorded by al-Nasaʼi and Abu Dawud, "Recite these two Surahs whenever you go to sleep and whenever you get up," and recited them himself in the prayer. Imam Malik records from ʿĀʼishah that whenever the Prophet ﷺ suffered an ailment he would recite the Muʿawwidhatayn over himself and blow; when his pain grew severe she would recite them and wipe his own hand over his body, seeking the blessing of these sūrahs — recorded by al-Bukhari, Abu Dawud, al-Nasaʼi and Ibn Majah. And Abu Saʿīd reports that the Prophet ﷺ used to seek protection against the evil eye of jinn and men by various means, but once the Muʿawwidhatayn were revealed he took them and abandoned everything else — recorded by al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasaʼi and Ibn Majah; al-Tirmidhi graded it Hasan Sahih.

Imam Ahmad also recorded, from Zirr bin Hubaysh, the report that Ibn Masʿūd did not write these two sūrahs in his own mushaf. Ubayy bin Kaʿb answered it decisively: "I testify that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ informed me that Jibril said to him, 'Say: I seek refuge with the Lord of al-Falaq'… so we say what the Prophet ﷺ said."

## Living this sūrah

The foundation, as Maʿārif states, is creed: Allah alone is the intrinsic cause of every gain and loss; without His will not a jot of gain or loss can reach anyone. So the only real fortress against harm — seen or unseen — is to place yourself under His protection. Ibn al-Qayyim writes that the blessings of these two sūrahs are so abundant that no one can dispense with them; grasped fully, a person would realise he needs them more than breath, food, water and clothing. The pair divide the work between them: al-Falaq teaches how to seek Allah's protection against the calamities of this world; al-Nās against the calamities of the Hereafter.

Concretely, from the hadith the sources cite: recite the Muʿawwidhatayn when you lie down and when you wake; the Prophet ﷺ also advised reciting them after every salah (transmitted by Abu Dawud and Nasaʼi); and ʿAbdullah ibn Khubayb reports that on a dark, rain-swept night the Prophet ﷺ told him to recite Sūrah al-Ikhlas and the Muʿawwidhatayn three times morning and evening, saying this would fortify him against all kinds of harm. And when illness strikes, recite them over yourself as the Prophet ﷺ did.

The sūrah ends where fear usually begins — with other people's malice — and answers it not with anxiety but with a Lord who splits open the dawn.
